Guided Inquiry

The coil in the field

A flat coil of N turns and area A carries current I in a uniform field B = 0.5 T. Its magnetic moment is μ = NIA, a vector along the coil's normal n̂, and θ is the angle from n̂ to B.

Each of the two side arms carries its current straight across the field, so each feels a force of magnitude F = NBIL.

What does the field do to the coil?

The uniform field acts on the current in all four arms of the coil. What does the coil do?

Where is the torque largest?

The coil starts with its plane along the field (θ = 90°) and turns to alignment (θ = 0°). At which angle is the torque largest?

Past alignment

Released from θ = 90°, the coil reaches alignment with the field. What happens next?

Doubling the turns

The number of turns N is doubled, with I, A and B unchanged. What changes?

The commutator

Reverse the current every half turn and the torque reverses with it, so it keeps driving the coil the same way round instead of dying at alignment.

The rotating contact that does this is a commutator — the reason a DC motor turns continuously.

Magnetic moment

N turns of area A carrying current I. Direction along the normal n̂, by the right-hand rule.

Torque on the coil

θ from the NORMAL to B. Restoring: signed −μB sin θ drives θ back to 0. τ_max = μB at θ = 90°; τ = 0 at θ = 0.

Potential energy

Minimum at θ = 0 (aligned), maximum at θ = 180° (anti-aligned). τ = −dU/dθ exactly.

Net force

In a UNIFORM field the two side-arm forces cancel — a pure couple. The coil turns; it does not translate.

The Physics

01

At a glance

A flat coil of N turns carries a current I and sits in a uniform magnetic field B, free to turn about a vertical axis. The sim draws the coil in 3-D, with its normal n̂ and the angle θ between n̂ and B, and it reads out four live values.

What you'll learn

  • Why a coil carrying current acts like a small magnet, and what sets its strength.
  • What a uniform magnetic field does to such a coil, and how that depends on the angle θ.
  • What happens as the coil reaches alignment, and what a motor does about it.
The coil seen edge-on from above. The normal n̂ makes the angle θ with the uniform field B.

03

A current loop is a magnetic moment

A coil of N turns, each of area A, carrying current I behaves like a small bar magnet. Its strength is the magnetic moment μ, and its direction is along the coil's normal n̂, which the right-hand rule fixes: curl your fingers along the current and your thumb points along n̂.

μ⃗ = N I A⃗, so μ = N I A
A⃗ has the coil's area as its length and n̂ as its direction.

The sim fixes A = 0.010 m². At the opening values N = 50 and I = 2.0 A the readout shows μ = 50 × 2.0 × 0.010 = 1.000 A·m². The angle θ is measured from n̂ to B, so at θ = 0° the moment points along the field and at θ = 180° it points against it.

See itSet N = 100 and I = 5.0 A. Watch for: the magnetic moment reading 5.000 A·m², and the coil still at θ = 90°.
04

A uniform field turns the coil without moving it

The field acts on the current in every arm of the coil. On each of the two side arms that cross the field the force has magnitude F = N B I L, where L is the length of an arm. The two forces are equal and opposite. The forces on the other two arms are equal, opposite and along one line, so they add no torque.

So the net force is F⃗net = 0 in a uniform field, and the coil does not drift. Because the two side forces act along different lines, a sideways distance apart, they form a couple. A couple is a pure torque: the coil turns on the spot.

The sim draws the two side-arm forces, labelled F, to scale. Their length does not change as the coil turns.

See itRelease the coil from θ = 90°. Watch for: the two F arrows keeping their length and pointing opposite ways, while the sideways gap between them opens and closes as the coil swings.
05

The torque follows sin θ

The lever arm of the couple is the coil's width b times sin θ. With the two forces F = N B I L, the torque is N B I L b sin θ, and since L b = A this is

τ⃗ = μ⃗ × B⃗, so |τ| = μ B sin θ
The sim shows τ with a sign: τ = −μB sin θ is negative because it pushes θ down toward 0°.

The torque is greatest, τmax = μB, at θ = 90°, where the coil's plane lies along the field. It is zero at θ = 0° and θ = 180°, where n̂ lies along the field line. With μ = 1.000 A·m² and B = 0.50 T that is −0.500 N·m at 90°, −0.250 N·m at 30° and 0 at 0°.

See itSet θ = 30° with N = 50 and I = 2.0 A. Watch for: the torque reading −0.250 N·m, half the peak torque of 0.500 N·m.
06

The coil overshoots alignment, then settles

The potential energy of the moment in the field is U = −μB cos θ. It is lowest at θ = 0°, the stable equilibrium, and highest at θ = 180°, the unstable one. The torque is −dU/dθ and is zero at both.

Released from θ = 90°, the coil speeds up toward θ = 0° and reaches it in about 0.38 s at 1× speed. It arrives with angular speed, so it carries on past alignment. There the torque reverses and slows it, then turns it back. The sim includes a little damping, so each swing is smaller: the first goes about 78° past alignment, the next about 68°.

The θ label shows only the size of the angle, so on the far side it climbs again from 0°. At θ = 180° nothing moves on Play, because τ = 0 there, but a small nudge would send the coil away.

See itRelease the coil from θ = 90°. Watch for: θ falling to 0° in about 0.4 s, then climbing again to about 78° before the coil swings back.
See itSet θ = 180° and press Play. Watch for: the coil staying put, with the state reading unstable equilibrium and τ = 0.
07

Turns and current set the strength, not the angles

More turns or more current raise μ = NIA, and with it the peak torque μB. The angles where the torque vanishes stay at θ = 0° and 180°, because sin θ = 0 depends only on the geometry. Neither N, I nor B can move them.

At θ = 90° and I = 2.0 A the peak torque is 0.500 N·m for N = 50 and 1.000 N·m for N = 100. A stronger torque also swings the coil faster: from θ = 90° it reaches alignment in about 0.38 s at N = 50 and about 0.27 s at N = 100.

See itSet N = 100 with θ = 90° and I = 2.0 A. Watch for: the torque and the peak torque both reading 1.000 N·m, twice the value at N = 50.
08

Where it matters

A DC motor is this coil in the field of a magnet, with its current supplied by a battery. With a steady current the torque dies as the coil reaches alignment, so the motor would swing a little and stop.

A motor turns continuously because a split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn. The torque then keeps its sense, and the coil is driven round instead of settling. The sim's Guided Inquiry shows this on its last card.

A moving-coil galvanometer uses the same torque, balanced by a spring: the deflection of the pointer measures the current. A compass needle is a magnetic moment that settles along the field in the same way.

09

Summary

In one line. A current loop is a magnetic moment μ = NIA along its normal, and a field B acts on it through the angle θ between the two.

Key points

  • μ = NIA points along n̂ by the right-hand rule, and θ is the angle from n̂ to B.
  • In a uniform field the net force is zero and the two side forces make a couple, so the coil turns without drifting.
  • |τ| = μB sin θ, greatest at 90° and zero at 0° and 180°. Its sense drives θ toward 0°.

Common mix-ups

  • "The field keeps pushing the coil round." It pushes only toward alignment. At θ = 0° the torque is zero.
  • "A field pulls a coil toward its stronger side." A uniform field has no stronger side, so the net force is zero.

Things to try on your own

  • Set θ = 45° and 135° and compare the torque readouts, then find which angles read 0.
  • Drop N to 1 with I = 0.2 A and watch how slowly the coil starts to move.
  • Release from θ = 20° and compare the swing with the one from 90°.
